name: Pakistan intends to integrate non-communicable diseases into primary health care

content.title: Pakistan intends to integrate non-communicable diseases into primary health care
content.summary: Non-communicable diseases - mainly hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, lung diseases and cancers - are now the leading cause of death and disability in Pakistan, causing premature deaths in the adult economically productive population.

content.text: Non-communicable diseases - mainly hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, lung diseases and cancers - are now the leading cause of death and disability in Pakistan, causing premature deaths in the adult economically productive population.

Today, three years after signing the Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of NCDs, Pakistan has announced its intention to fully integrate NCDs into the primary health care system by establishing non-communicable diseases' units at the federal and provincial levels.

Experts believe that this is a major step towards dealing with NCDs at the first stage of health care: moving towards preventive care - helping a person avoid illnesses - rather than focusing on curative services. NCD units would screen adults when they visit a health facility and shift health interventions from specialists to certified family physicians, general physicians and other frontline providers, backed by training and treatment protocols.

The announcement was made at a workshop in Islamabad, where health experts had gathered to discuss a harmonised response to NCDs in the light of research study conducted by the Aga Khan University and funded by the World Health Organization's Office of the Eastern Mediterranean Region. On the occasion, the Ministry of Health launched its NCD Unit and also announced designated focal persons in each of the provinces.

The study is a regional situation analysis of NCD integration into the primary health care systems of countries in the WHO EMRO region as well as five in-depth country case studies covering Pakistan, Iran, Jordan, Morocco and Oman.

"While most countries have made a solid beginning in integrating NCD conditions into primary care services, moving towards consolidation will require more effort. Most regional countries have very basic services for diabetes and hypertension at the primary health care level and will need to expand to include cardiovascular diseases screening, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease early management and cancer screening," said Dr Shehla Zaidi, the study investigator and an associate professor at the Aga Khan University.

"Pakistan needs to decide on the breadth and depth of the four NCD conditions and mainstream the NCD services into the health reform agendas that have started out in the provinces. These services include contracting out, regulatory commissions as well as the national health insurance package. A dedicated cadre of family physicians will be needed as well as an expansion in the workforce of pharmacists, health educators and nutritionists at district hubs to support the primary health care networks. Enhancement of operational budgets, pooling from employers and a proportion of the tax from cigarettes and carbonated drinks are some ways to mobilise additional resources. NCDs need to be horizontally integrated rather than setting up more vertical structures in an already fragmented public health care network," she added.

"NCDs need to be at the centre of the development agenda post the MDGs, with a broad coalition of stakeholders - whole-of-society - mobilised around this human development challenge," said Dr Asad Hafeez, Director General Health, Ministry of National Health Services Regulations and Coordination, Government of Pakistan. "The way forward is to implement the NCD action plans in consultation with all stakeholders, advocate at all levels and increase funding for the health sector."

Other speakers included Dr Malik Muhammad Safi, Director and National Focal Person for NCDs and Muhammad Ayub Sheikh, Secretary, MoNHSRC; Dr Haroon Jahangir Khan, Director NCDs and Mental Health, Division of Health, Government of Punjab; and Dr Samer Jabour, Regional Director, NCDs, WHO EMRO.

The audience was made up of health experts from MoNHSRC; provincial focal persons for non-communicable diseases; representatives from WHO Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office; and experts from the Aga Khan University.
